questions.qa_note: concept: guide 3.5 (advantages and disadvantages of ownership)

questions.stem: A company declares a dividend with a record date on a Wednesday. Monday to Friday are business days, and settlement is T+1. What is the last day a client can buy the shares and get the dividend?

options.A: The Monday before the record date
options.B: The Wednesday that is the record date
options.C: The Tuesday before the record date
options.D: The Thursday after the record date

questions.rationale: Settlement is T+1, so a trade must occur at least one business day before the record date. A Tuesday trade settles on Wednesday, in time. A Wednesday trade settles on Thursday, too late. The ex-dividend date is normally the record date itself.
questions.source_quote: "Current SRO and marketplace rules mandate a standard T+1 settlement cycle period for most transactions in equity and long term debt securities." — research/sources/csa/cp-24-101-institutional-trade-matching-and-settlement-companion-policy.txt 24-101CP s.5.1, ~L461

questions.stem: Ines Marchetti holds 600 shares at $90 each. The company does a 3-for-1 stock split. Which statement correctly describes her position after the split?

options.A: She has 1,800 shares at about $90, and her total value triples
options.B: She has 200 shares at about $270, and the split is not taxable
options.C: She has 1,800 shares at about $30, and the split is not taxable
options.D: She has 1,800 shares at about $30, and the split is a taxable disposition

questions.rationale: A 3-for-1 split triples the number of shares and divides the price by three. Her total value and percentage ownership do not change. CRA treats a split as no disposition, so it is not taxable. She must recalculate her ACB per share.
questions.source_quote: "no stock dividend is considered to have been issued, no disposition or acquisition is considered to have occurred and the event is not taxable." — research/sources/cra/guide-t4037-capital-gains-2025.txt T4037 Stock splits and consolidations, ~L1795-1798

questions.stem: Tobias Lund receives eligible dividends from a taxable Canadian corporation in a non-registered account. Which statement describes the federal tax treatment?

options.A: He reports 115% of the dividends and claims a credit of 9/13 of the gross-up
options.B: He reports the actual dividends and claims no dividend tax credit
options.C: He reports 138% of the dividends and claims no dividend tax credit
options.D: He reports 138% of the dividends and claims a credit of 6/11 of the gross-up

questions.rationale: Eligible dividends get a 38% gross-up, so 138% is taxable (ITA s. 82). The federal dividend tax credit is 6/11 of the gross-up (s. 121). The 115% and 9/13 figures apply to dividends other than eligible dividends.
questions.source_quote: "(D) for taxation years that end after 2011, 38%;" — research/sources/gov/ita-dividends-gross-up-dtc.txt ITA s.82(1)(b)(ii)(D), ~L18

questions.stem: Granville Utilities Inc. buys back its own shares through a normal-course issuer bid on the TSX. Its total earnings stay the same. What is the usual effect on the shareholders who do not sell?

options.A: EPS usually decreases, because the bid uses the company's cash
options.B: Each remaining holder owns a smaller percentage, because of dilution
options.C: EPS usually increases, and each remaining holder owns a larger percentage
options.D: Each remaining holder gets a taxable distribution of the bid cash

questions.rationale: A buyback reduces the number of shares outstanding. If earnings do not decrease, EPS usually increases. The remaining shareholders own a larger percentage of the company. Only the shareholders who sell receive cash. Dilution comes from new shares, not from a buyback.

questions.stem: Tremont Mills Inc. has cumulative preferred shares. It skipped four quarterly preferred dividends. Its board now wants to declare a dividend on the common shares. What must Tremont do first?

options.A: Pay all of the unpaid preferred dividends
options.B: Pay only the current quarter's preferred dividend
options.C: Nothing, because skipped preferred dividends are lost
options.D: Cure the default that the skipped dividends caused

questions.rationale: On cumulative preferred shares, missed dividends accumulate as arrears. The issuer must pay all arrears before any common dividend. Skipped dividends are lost only on non-cumulative shares. A missed preferred dividend is not a default.

questions.stem: Which preferred share feature gives the holder the right to sell the shares back to the issuer at a set price on set dates?

options.A: Redeemable
options.B: Retractable
options.C: Convertible
options.D: Participating

questions.rationale: A retractable feature is a put for the holder, who can sell back at a set price on set dates. A redeemable (callable) feature is the opposite: the issuer can buy the shares back. A convertible exchanges into common shares. A participating share gets extra dividends.

questions.stem: Mireille Fontaine expects interest rates to rise. She holds four preferred shares of similar credit quality. Which share is most exposed to a fall in price?

options.A: A floating-rate preferred tied to a reference interest rate
options.B: A straight perpetual preferred with a fixed dividend
options.C: A retractable preferred with a retraction date next year
options.D: A fixed-reset preferred whose rate resets next month

questions.rationale: When rates rise, fixed-dividend prices fall. A straight perpetual has no maturity to pull its price back to par, so it is most exposed. A floating-rate dividend rises with rates. A retraction right lets the holder sell back at a set price. A reset next month raises the rate soon.

questions.stem: Lukas Brenner holds a callable preferred share. It trades slightly above its call price. Interest rates then fall further. Which outcome is most likely?

options.A: The price rises without limit as rates continue to fall
options.B: The issuer must keep the shares outstanding at least until maturity
options.C: He can force the issuer to buy back the shares at par
options.D: The price rises little, and the issuer may redeem the shares

questions.rationale: A call feature caps the gain, because the price rarely rises far above the call price. When rates fall, the issuer can redeem the shares: this is call risk. A forced sale back to the issuer is a retraction right, which belongs to the holder of a retractable share.

questions.stem: Calder Freight Ltd. compares two ways to raise the same amount: preferred shares or bonds. Which disadvantage applies to the preferred shares but not to the bonds?

options.A: Calder pays the dividends from after-tax profit, but interest is generally deductible
options.B: A skipped preferred dividend puts Calder into legal default with the holders
options.C: Preferred shareholders vote on all ordinary matters at every shareholder meeting
options.D: The preferred shares increase Calder's debt-to-equity ratio after the issue

questions.rationale: Preferred dividends come out of after-tax profit, whereas interest is generally a deductible expense. So preferreds usually cost more than debt. A skipped preferred dividend is not a default. Preferreds usually carry no vote, and they add equity, so debt-to-equity improves.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 3.9 (advantages and disadvantages to the issuer)

questions.stem: Noor Haddad is 67 and wants steady income in her taxable account. She also wants priority over common shareholders if the issuer has problems. Which choice fits her better, and why?

options.A: Common shares, because their dividends are fixed and the board cannot cut them
options.B: Preferred shares, because a missed dividend lets her force the issuer into default
options.C: Common shares, because they rank ahead of preferred shares on dissolution
options.D: Preferred shares, because their dividends have priority and may get the dividend tax credit

questions.rationale: Preferred dividends come before any common dividend, and the stated amount ranks ahead of common on dissolution. In a taxable account, dividends from taxable Canadian corporations may qualify for the dividend tax credit. A missed preferred dividend is not a default. Common dividends are discretionary.
questions.source_quote: "You may be able to claim a dividend tax credit on line 40425 for dividends received from taxable Canadian corporations." — research/sources/cra/investment-income-interest-dividends-foreign-tax-credit.txt CRA Lines 12000/12010 Tax Tips, ~L240

questions.stem: Liesl Varga considers a straight perpetual preferred share that pays $1.50 a year. She requires a 6% return. What is the share's value using the zero-growth model?
questions.rationale: The zero-growth model values a constant dividend paid forever: P₀ = D ÷ r = 1.50 ÷ 0.06 = $25.00. The $26.50 answer wrongly grows the dividend by 6% first. The $9.00 answer multiplies instead of divides.

questions.stem: Dorian Feld looks at a common share that just paid a $1.50 dividend. He expects dividends to grow 5% a year forever and requires an 11% return. What is the share's value using the constant-growth model?
questions.rationale: The Gordon model uses next year's dividend: D₁ = 1.50 × 1.05 = 1.575. So P₀ = 1.575 ÷ (0.11 − 0.05) = $26.25. The $25.00 answer wrongly uses D₀. The $14.32 answer leaves growth out of the denominator.

questions.stem: Analysts forecast next year's EPS for Ridgeback Tools Inc. at $4.00. The payout ratio is 50%, the required return is 12% and growth is 7%. The share trades at $46.00. What is the model value from the justified P/E, and how does the share look?

options.A: $40.00, so the share looks undervalued
options.B: $80.00, so the share looks undervalued
options.C: $40.00, so the share looks overvalued
options.D: $28.57, so the share looks overvalued

questions.rationale: Justified P/E = 0.50 ÷ (0.12 − 0.07) = 10, so P₀ = 4.00 × 10 = $40.00. The market price of $46.00 is above the model value, so the share looks overvalued. The $80.00 answer leaves out the payout ratio.

questions.stem: Kestrel Grain Corp., a reporting issuer, has a material change. Under NI 51-102, when must it file its material change report?

options.A: Within 45 days after the end of the current quarter
options.B: Within 90 days after the end of its financial year
options.C: As soon as practicable, and within 10 days of the change
options.D: Only after the board of directors confirms the change

questions.rationale: NI 51-102 s. 7.1(1)(b) requires the report as soon as practicable, and in any event within 10 days of the change. The 45-day and 90-day periods are deadlines for interim and annual statements.
questions.source_quote: "as soon as practicable, and in any event within 10 days of the date on which the change occurs" — research/sources/csa/ni-51-102-continuous-disclosure-obligations.txt NI 51-102 s. 7.1(1)(b), ~line 2487

questions.stem: Lodestar Cobalt Inc. signs a contract that would reasonably be expected to have a significant effect on its share price. What must it do immediately?

options.A: Tell its largest shareholders first, then issue a news release within 10 days
options.B: Ask the exchange for a trading halt and wait for the next interim report
options.C: Describe the change in its next MD&A and its next Annual Information Form
options.D: Issue and file a news release, authorized by an executive officer, on the change

questions.rationale: A material change requires an immediate news release on its nature and substance (NI 51-102 s. 7.1(1)(a)). An executive officer must authorize it. Telling large shareholders first is selective disclosure, which can create insider trading opportunities.
questions.source_quote: "the reporting issuer must (a) immediately issue and file a news release authorized by an executive officer disclosing the nature and substance of the change" — research/sources/csa/ni-51-102-continuous-disclosure-obligations.txt NI 51-102 s. 7.1(1)(a), ~line 2484

questions.stem: Thornbury Metals Ltd. filed a confidential material change report on a planned takeover. A week later, it learns that some people trade its shares with knowledge of the deal. What must Thornbury do?

options.A: Keep the report confidential and mention the trading in its next 10-day update
options.B: Keep the report confidential until the board confirms the planned takeover
options.C: Promptly make general disclosure of the material change to the public
options.D: Tell only the people who traded to stop trading in its shares

questions.rationale: People trade with knowledge of the change. So the issuer must promptly generally disclose it (NI 51-102 s. 7.1(7)). Confidentiality with 10-day updates (s. 7.1(5)) is then no longer an option.
questions.source_quote: "the reporting issuer must promptly generally disclose the material change in the manner referred to in subsection (1) upon the reporting issuer becoming aware, or having reasonable grounds to believe, that persons or companies are purchasing or selling securities" — research/sources/csa/ni-51-102-continuous-disclosure-obligations.txt NI 51-102 s. 7.1(7), ~line 2532

questions.stem: RR Oksana Vellacott emails one client: "Halberd Tech shares will reach $40 by June." The email gives no other context. Which rule problem does this email have?

options.A: It states a forecast of future events that is not clearly labelled as such
options.B: It is correspondence, so the dealer content rules do not apply to it
options.C: It is a research report, so it must first disclose the valuation method
options.D: It gives material nonpublic information to a single client only

questions.rationale: An email to one client is correspondence (IDPC 1201(2)). IDPC 3602(1)(iv) bans correspondence with an opinion or forecast that is not clearly labelled as such. So the content rules do apply to correspondence.
questions.source_quote: "contains any opinion or forecast of future events which is not clearly labeled as such" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3602(1)(iv), ~line 7288

questions.stem: A dealer's research report rates Fenwick Solar Inc. a buy. The dealer was paid to underwrite a Fenwick share issue ten months before the report. What does IDPC 3608 require?

options.A: The report needs no disclosure, because the fee was paid over six months ago
options.B: The report discloses the paid investment banking services as a possible conflict
options.C: The dealer withdraws the rating until 12 months pass after the share issue
options.D: The RR discloses the services only if a client asks about conflicts

questions.rationale: IDPC 3608(2)(iv) requires disclosure of paid investment banking services from the dealer to the issuer in the 12 months before the report. Ten months is inside that period. The rule requires disclosure, not withdrawal of the rating.
questions.source_quote: "any investment banking services provided by the Dealer Member to the issuer for remuneration during the 12 months immediately preceding the date a research report or recommendation was issued" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3608(2)(iv), ~line 7381

questions.stem: How does the statement of changes in equity link a company's financial statements?

options.A: Operating cash flow flows into share capital, and closing equity equals cash
options.B: Revenue flows into contributed surplus, and closing equity equals market capitalization
options.C: Net income flows into retained earnings, and closing equity equals balance-sheet equity
options.D: Dividends flow into net income, and closing equity equals total assets

questions.rationale: The statement adds net income and OCI, deducts dividends, and adjusts for share issues and buybacks. Its closing totals equal equity on the balance sheet. Equity is a book amount, not cash or market capitalization.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.2 statement of changes in equity

questions.stem: On a statement of financial position, which item is a current liability?

options.A: Long-term debt that is due in five years
options.B: The portion of long-term debt that is due within 12 months
options.C: Deferred tax liabilities that reverse in later years
options.D: Lease liabilities that are due after the next 12 months

questions.rationale: Current items are items that the company expects to settle within 12 months or one operating cycle. So the current portion of long-term debt is current. Deferred tax liabilities and debt due in five years are non-current.

questions.stem: On the statement of comprehensive income, which subtotal shows the result before the effect of debt financing and tax?

options.A: Gross profit (revenue less cost of goods sold)
options.B: EBIT (operating income plus or minus other income)
options.C: Earnings before tax (EBIT less finance costs)
options.D: Net income (earnings before tax less income tax)

questions.rationale: EBIT comes before finance costs and income tax, so it shows the result before debt financing and tax. Earnings before tax already deducts interest. Gross profit shows only the cost of making or buying products.

questions.stem: Which item does a company record in other comprehensive income (OCI), outside profit?

options.A: A gain on the sale of one of its business divisions
options.B: Foreign-currency translation differences on its foreign operations
options.C: Interest that it earns on its cash balances
options.D: Royalties that it earns from licensing its patents

questions.rationale: OCI items, such as foreign-currency translation differences, are recorded outside profit and are mostly unrealized. Interest earned is other income, and royalties are operating revenue. A gain on the sale of a division stays inside profit.

questions.stem: Under the indirect method, how does an increase in accounts receivable affect cash flow from operating activities?

options.A: It is subtracted, because the company has not yet collected the cash
options.B: It is added, because credit sales increase the net income
options.C: It is added back, because it is a non-cash charge like depreciation
options.D: It is excluded, because receivables belong in investing activities

questions.rationale: An increase in receivables uses cash, so the indirect method subtracts it from net income. The company recorded the revenue, but customers have not paid. Depreciation is a non-cash charge, but a receivables increase is a working-capital change.

questions.stem: Which cash flow pattern is the strongest warning sign about a company?

options.A: Negative investing cash flow from capital spending in a growing company
options.B: Negative financing cash flow from dividends and debt repayment in a mature company
options.C: Negative operating cash flow every year, with new borrowing each year to cover it
options.D: Positive financing cash flow in a young company that builds new plant

questions.rationale: A financing inflow that pays for operating losses does not fix the business. It only delays the problem. A young company that raises cash to invest, or a mature company that pays lenders and shareholders, shows a normal pattern.

questions.stem: An auditor's report says that the financial statements present fairly, except for one specific matter. What type of opinion is this?

options.A: A qualified opinion
options.B: An unmodified opinion
options.C: An adverse opinion
options.D: A disclaimer of opinion

questions.rationale: A qualified opinion means that the statements are fair except for a specific matter. An unmodified opinion has no exception. An adverse opinion says that the statements are not fairly presented. A disclaimer means the auditor lacked evidence.

questions.stem: Ravensworth Foods Inc. files an interim financial report. No auditor reviewed it. What does NI 51-102 require?

options.A: A full audit of the report before the company can file it
options.B: A notice with the report that says no auditor reviewed it
options.C: A qualified audit opinion that the company attaches to the report
options.D: A delay of the filing until the annual audit is complete

questions.rationale: If no auditor reviewed an interim report, NI 51-102 s. 4.3(3) requires a notice that says so. Only annual financial statements must be audited (s. 4.1(2)). So a full audit of the interim report is not required.
questions.source_quote: "accompanied by a notice indicating that the interim financial report has not been reviewed by an auditor" — research/sources/csa/ni-51-102-continuous-disclosure-obligations.txt NI 51-102 s. 4.3(3)(a), ~line 890

questions.stem: Ashgrove Tools Ltd. has cash of $60M, marketable securities of $40M, receivables of $140M and inventory of $300M. Its current liabilities are $360M. What is its quick ratio?
questions.rationale: Quick ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities = (540 − 300) ÷ 360 = 0.67. The value 1.50 is the current ratio, which includes inventory. The value 0.28 is the cash ratio.

questions.stem: Brackenridge Freight Inc. has EBIT of $96M and interest expense of $24M. In a recession, assume that EBIT falls by 50% and interest does not change. What is the new interest coverage, and what does it show?

options.A: 4.0×; profit covers interest with a wide safety margin
options.B: 0.5×; profit is too low to cover the interest expense
options.C: 2.0×; profit still covers interest, but the safety margin is thin
options.D: 3.0×; profit covers interest with a moderate safety margin

questions.rationale: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest = (96 × 0.5) ÷ 24 = 2.0×. EBIT still covers interest twice, but a further fall would threaten payment. The value 4.0× is the coverage before the recession.

questions.stem: Over three years, Corvallis Brands Inc. keeps a gross margin near 38%. Its net margin falls from 9% to 6%. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Price cuts on its products to win market share
options.B: Higher overhead, interest or income tax costs
options.C: Higher purchase costs for its raw materials
options.D: A sales shift toward its low-margin products

questions.rationale: Gross margin reflects prices, input costs and product mix. It is stable, so these did not change much. A lower net margin with a stable gross margin points to overhead, interest or tax.

questions.stem: Delmore Home Goods Inc. had inventory turnover of 7.0× and then 6.0× in the last two years. This year, COGS is $960M and year-end inventory is $240M. What does the trend suggest?

options.A: Turnover is 4.0×; inventory sells faster, which helps liquidity
options.B: Turnover is 6.0×; the company uses its inventory as before
options.C: Turnover is 4.0×; weaker demand or obsolete inventory is possible
options.D: Turnover is 0.25×; the company holds too little inventory

questions.rationale: Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ inventory = 960 ÷ 240 = 4.0×. It fell from 7.0× to 6.0× to 4.0×, so inventory sells more slowly. Lower turnover over several periods signals weaker demand or obsolete inventory.

questions.stem: Ellesmere Packaging Ltd. reports operating cash flow of $420M and capex of $310M. It repaid a net $40M of debt and paid dividends of $90M. What is its FCFE, and does it cover the dividend?

options.A: $150M; FCFE covers the dividend with room to spare
options.B: $110M; FCFE covers the dividend with a small margin
options.C: −$20M; the company cannot pay any dividend at all
options.D: $70M; FCFE does not cover the $90M dividend

questions.rationale: FCFE = operating cash flow − capex + net borrowing = 420 − 310 − 40 = $70M. Net debt repayment is negative borrowing, so it reduces FCFE. FCFE of $70M is below the $90M dividend.

questions.stem: Fairhaven Grocers Inc. trades at $27.00. Its EPS is $1.80, and its dividends per share are $0.54. What is its P/E ratio?
questions.rationale: P/E = price ÷ EPS = 27.00 ÷ 1.80 = 15.0×. The value 50.0× divides the price by the dividend, not by EPS. The value 3.3× is the dividend cover, EPS ÷ DPS.

questions.stem: Glenbrook Steel Corp. shares fell from $36 to $18. It pays dividends of $1.26 a share, and its EPS is $0.90. Client Ottilie Marchetti wants to buy for the yield. What is the best assessment?

options.A: Yield is 3.5% and cover is 1.40×, so the dividend is safe
options.B: Yield is 7.0% and cover is 0.71×, so a dividend cut is a real risk
options.C: Yield is 7.0% and cover is 1.40×, so earnings cover the dividend well
options.D: Yield is 5.0% and cover is 0.71×, so the yield is below average

questions.rationale: Dividend yield = 1.26 ÷ 18 = 7.0%. Dividend cover = EPS ÷ DPS = 0.90 ÷ 1.26 = 0.71×, so the dividend exceeds earnings. The high yield comes from the price fall. The value 1.40× inverts the cover formula.

questions.stem: Harwick Software Inc. reported EPS of $2.00, $2.40 and $2.76 over the last three years. Which statement about the trend is correct?

options.A: EPS rises each year, by a larger percentage each year
options.B: EPS rises each year, by the same 20% each year
options.C: EPS rises each year, by the same $0.40 each year
options.D: EPS rises each year, but by a smaller percentage each year

questions.rationale: EPS growth is (2.40 − 2.00) ÷ 2.00 = 20%, then (2.76 − 2.40) ÷ 2.40 = 15%. EPS rises, but the rate of growth slows. The dollar increase also falls, from $0.40 to $0.36.

questions.stem: A securities regulator issued a cease trade order (CTO) against Ironvale Gold Ltd. The CTO is still in effect. Client Leopold Haverty asks his RR to buy the shares over-the-counter. What should the RR tell him?

options.A: The RR can execute the order over-the-counter, because the CTO applies only to exchanges
options.B: The RR can execute the order on the TSX if the client accepts the risk in writing
options.C: No order can be executed on a marketplace or over-the-counter while the CTO is in effect
options.D: The RR can execute the order once the company files a news release on the CTO

questions.rationale: UMIR 9.1(1)(a) bans the execution of any order on a marketplace or over-the-counter while a CTO remains in effect. Client consent does not override the ban. The CTO stays until the regulator revokes it.
questions.source_quote: "an order of a securities regulatory authority to cease trading in the security, derivative, related security or related derivative remains in effect" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 9.1(1)(a), ~line 12060

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes who imposes each type of trading stop?

options.A: CIRO issues a CTO, and a securities regulator imposes a regulatory halt
options.B: The exchange issues a CTO, and the company imposes a regulatory halt
options.C: A securities regulator issues a CTO, and CIRO imposes a regulatory halt
options.D: The company issues a CTO, and the exchange imposes a regulatory halt

questions.rationale: A CTO comes from a securities regulator. After a CSA regulator issues a CTO, CIRO, the market regulator, imposes a regulatory halt (NP 11-207 s. 12).
questions.source_quote: "if a CSA regulator issues a cease trade order with respect to an issuer whose securities are traded on a marketplace, IIROC imposes a regulatory halt on trading of those securities on all marketplaces for which IIROC acts as the regulation services provider" — research/sources/csa/np-11-207-failure-to-file-cease-trade-orders.txt NP 11-207 s. 12, ~line 327

questions.stem: In a price-weighted index, which constituent stock has the largest effect on the index level?

options.A: The stock with the highest share price
options.B: The stock with the largest market capitalization
options.C: The stock with the largest public float
options.D: The stock with the most trading volume

questions.rationale: In a price-weighted index, each stock's weight is proportional to its share price, regardless of company size. Market capitalization and float decide weights in a cap-weighted, float-adjusted index such as the S&P/TSX Composite.

questions.stem: Which statement about an equal-weighted index is correct?

options.A: It gives the largest companies the most weight in the index
options.B: It sets each stock's weight in proportion to its share price
options.C: It never needs rebalancing, because its weights stay equal
options.D: It needs regular rebalancing and tilts toward smaller companies

questions.rationale: An equal-weighted index gives every stock the same weight. Prices move apart, so it needs rebalancing to restore equal weights. Compared with a cap-weighted index, it tilts toward smaller companies.

questions.stem: Client Rosalind Achebe has a 70/30 balanced portfolio that returned 7.0% last year. The equity total-return index gained 10.0%, and the bond universe total-return index gained 2.0%. How did the portfolio perform against a blended benchmark?

options.A: It underperformed by 0.6 percentage points
options.B: It outperformed by 1.0 percentage point
options.C: It underperformed by 3.0 percentage points
options.D: It outperformed by 5.0 percentage points

questions.rationale: Blended benchmark = 0.70 × 10.0% + 0.30 × 2.0% = 7.6%. Relative return = 7.0% − 7.6% = −0.6 points. A comparison with the equity index alone (−3.0 points) ignores the 30% bond weight.

questions.stem: RR Casimir Lindqvist manages a broad Canadian equity portfolio with a total return of 6.5%. The S&P/TSX Composite had a price return of 4.0% and a total return of 7.0%. What is the correct relative return?

options.A: +2.5 points, against the price-return index
options.B: −0.5 points, against the total-return index
options.C: +0.5 points, against the total-return index
options.D: −2.5 points, against the price-return index

questions.rationale: The portfolio's 6.5% includes dividends, so compare it with the total-return index: 6.5% − 7.0% = −0.5 points. A price-return benchmark omits dividends and makes the portfolio look 2.5 points better.

questions.stem: Analyst Wendeline Ostrowski says that Kingsmere Rail's shares are below their 200-day moving average and near a support level. She does not use financial statements. Which assumption underlies her method?

options.A: Prices move toward intrinsic value, which depends on forecast cash flows
options.B: The peer group is fairly priced, so a relative P/E shows value
options.C: Markets are efficient, so no method can earn abnormal returns
options.D: Prices adjust gradually to information, so trends persist and patterns repeat

questions.rationale: Moving averages and support levels are technical analysis tools. Technical analysis assumes that prices adjust gradually, so they move in trends and patterns repeat. The intrinsic-value assumption belongs to fundamental analysis.

questions.stem: A dealer's research report sets a $75 price target on Lakehurst Pipelines Inc., which trades at $58. Client Thaddeus Nkemelu asks whether the target is reliable. What should his RR do?

options.A: Accept the target, because a dealer's research report is a public filing
options.B: Find the disclosed valuation method, then test the key assumptions behind it
options.C: Compare the target with the stock's 200-day moving average only
options.D: Tell the client that targets need no stated method, so none can be tested

questions.rationale: If a dealer sets a price target in a research report, IDPC 3616(1) requires the report to disclose the valuation method. The RR can then test assumptions such as growth or the discount rate. Research is opinion, not a filing.
questions.source_quote: "If a Dealer Member sets a price target in a research report, the Dealer Member must disclose, in that research report, the valuation method used." — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3616(1), ~line 7459

questions.stem: Why do analysts often value a manufacturing company on its average earnings over a full cycle?

options.A: High fixed costs make profits swing widely, so one year's P/E can mislead
options.B: Its assets are mainly financial, so price-to-book is a better measure
options.C: Regulation fixes its revenue, so one year's earnings show the full picture
options.D: It pays no dividends, so the P/E ratio cannot be calculated for it

questions.rationale: Manufacturers have high fixed costs, so a small change in sales gives a large change in profit. One year's P/E can mislead at the top of the cycle. Price-to-book suits banks, whose assets are mainly financial.

questions.stem: A quarterly report shows that productivity rose faster than economists expected, while wages grew steadily. What is the most likely market effect?

options.A: Margins improve and inflation pressure eases, giving the central bank room to hold rates
options.B: Inflation pressure rises, so the central bank must raise rates sooner
options.C: Unit labour costs rise, so company margins and earnings fall
options.D: Bond prices fall, because higher output always pushes yields up

questions.rationale: Productivity is output per hour of work. If it rises faster than wages, unit labour costs fall, so margins improve without higher prices. The economy can grow with less inflation, so the central bank has room to hold rates.

questions.stem: Client Benedikt Szabo plans to hold equities for 25 years. Which statement about his long time horizon is correct?

options.A: It removes the risk of a loss in any single year of the period
options.B: It narrows the range of final dollar wealth that he can expect
options.C: It makes his expected equity return equal to the return on bonds
options.D: It narrows the spread of average annual returns, but not the risk of a loss in any year

questions.rationale: Over long horizons, the spread of average annual returns narrows. But the range of final dollar wealth does not narrow, and a loss can still occur in any single year. Equities keep the highest expected return.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.14 volatility and exam trap

questions.stem: Under securities law, which feature makes an investment fund a mutual fund, and not a non-redeemable investment fund?

options.A: Its securities give the holder a right to redeem on demand at an amount based on net assets.
options.B: Its securities trade on a stock exchange at a price that supply and demand set.
options.C: It invests money from many investors under the direction of a professional manager.
options.D: It distributes all of its net income and net capital gains to investors each year.

questions.rationale: A mutual fund's securities entitle the holder to receive, on demand, an amount based on the fund's net assets. A non-redeemable investment fund also pools investor money under a manager. So pooling does not separate the two, but the redemption right does.
questions.source_quote: "“mutual fund” means an issuer whose primary purpose is to invest money provided by its security holders and whose securities entitle the holder to receive on demand, or within a specified period after demand, an amount computed by reference to the value of a proportionate interest" — research/sources/gov/ontario-securities-act-extracts.txt Securities Act (Ontario) s.1(1) 'mutual fund', ~L180

questions.stem: A closed-end fund and an ETF both trade on a stock exchange. Why can the closed-end fund trade at a persistent discount to NAV, while the ETF usually does not?

options.A: The ETF must calculate its NAV each hour, but the closed-end fund calculates it once a year.
options.B: The closed-end fund must hold only illiquid assets, but the ETF must hold only index securities.
options.C: The ETF has a creation and redemption process that lets authorized dealers keep its price near NAV.
options.D: The closed-end fund cannot pay distributions, but the ETF must pay distributions each month.

questions.rationale: Only an ETF has a creation and redemption process. Authorized dealers use it for arbitrage when the price moves away from NAV. A closed-end fund issues units mainly at its IPO, so supply does not adjust and a discount can persist.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.1 exam trap and 5.5 creation and redemption

questions.stem: Priya buys shares of a mutual fund corporation in a non-registered account. Which tax slip does she receive for the fund's distributions?

options.A: A T3 slip, because the fund passes its income through to her as a trust
options.B: A T5 slip, because the corporation pays dividends and capital gains dividends
options.C: No slip, because the corporation pays the tax on all income inside the fund
options.D: Both a T3 slip and a T5 slip, because she holds both units and shares

questions.rationale: A mutual fund corporation issues shares and pays dividends and capital gains dividends, which it reports on a T5 slip. A mutual fund trust issues units and gives a T3 slip. Priya holds shares of a corporation, so the T3 answer is wrong.
rule_refs: CRA Tax treatment of mutual funds
questions.source_quote: "If you own units of a mutual fund trust, the trust will give you a T3 slip, Statement of Trust Income Allocations and Designations. If you own shares of a mutual fund corporation, the corporation will give you a T5 slip" — research/sources/cra/capital-gains-losses-superficial-loss-pages.txt CRA 'Tax treatment of mutual funds' — How income is taxed, ~L1604

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund holds 9% of its NAV in securities of one issuer. The portfolio manager wants to buy more, which would take the position to 12% of NAV. For which issuer is this purchase permitted?

options.A: A Canadian chartered bank, through its common shares
options.B: A utility company, through its senior bonds
options.C: A mining company, through its preferred shares
options.D: The Government of Canada, through its bonds

questions.rationale: A conventional mutual fund must not buy a security if more than 10% of its NAV would then be in one issuer. The limit does not apply to a government security. A corporate bond is still a security of one issuer, so the utility purchase breaks the limit.
questions.source_quote: "(a) a government security;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.1(2)(a), ~L1050

questions.stem: Malik holds 75% of his account in one energy fund with 50 stocks. He asks his RR to buy more and says, "A fund is always diversified." Which assessment is most accurate?

options.A: The fund holds 50 stocks, so the account is diversified, and concentration is not a suitability factor here.
options.B: The fund obeys the 10% single-issuer limit, so the dealer may treat the whole account as diversified.
options.C: The fund spreads risk over many issuers, but the account is concentrated in one sector, and the dealer must consider this.
options.D: Concentration applies only to individual stocks, so the dealer may accept the order with no further review.

questions.rationale: A sector fund spreads money over many issuers, but one sector shock hits the whole holding. The single-issuer limit counts issuers, not sectors. Under IDPC 3402(1), the dealer must consider the concentration of securities in the account.
questions.source_quote: "the impact of the action on the retail client’s account, including the concentration of securities, derivatives or precious metals bullion, within the account and the liquidity of those securities, derivatives or precious metals bullion," — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3402(1)(i)(c), ~L6803

questions.stem: Which statement about who holds a mutual fund's portfolio assets is correct?

options.A: A custodian holds them, and the manager must not act as custodian of the fund.
options.B: The manager holds them, because the manager directs the business of the fund.
options.C: The principal distributor holds them, because it sells the units of the fund.
options.D: Each participating dealer holds the assets that belong to its own clients.

questions.rationale: The portfolio assets are held under the custodianship of one custodian. NI 81-102 says that the manager must not act as custodian or sub-custodian. This split protects investors, because the firm that directs the fund does not also hold its assets.
questions.source_quote: "Despite any other provisions of this Part, the manager of an investment fund must not act as custodian or sub-custodian of the investment fund." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-part-6-custodianship-part-11-commingling-of-cash.txt NI 81-102 s.6.1(6), ~L84

questions.stem: Ravi places an order to buy units of a mutual fund on Tuesday, after the daily cut-off time. The fund treats late orders as received on the next business day. At which price does the fund fill his order?

options.A: The NAVPS that the fund calculated at the close on Monday
options.B: The NAVPS that the fund calculates at the close on Tuesday
options.C: The market price at the time that the fund receives the order
options.D: The NAVPS that the fund calculates at the close on Wednesday

questions.rationale: Under forward pricing, the fund uses the NAVPS next determined after it receives the order. The fund treats Ravi's late order as received on Wednesday, so Wednesday's NAVPS applies. Forward pricing stops investors from buying at a known, stale price.
questions.source_quote: "The issue price of a security of a mutual fund to which a purchase order pertains must be the net asset value per security of that class, or series of a class, next determined after the receipt by the mutual fund of the order." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.9.3(1), ~L2408

questions.stem: A mutual fund uses specified derivatives to hedge its currency risk. Under NI 81-106, what is the minimum frequency at which it must calculate its NAV?

options.A: Once a week
options.B: Every business day
options.C: Once a month
options.D: At each quarter end

questions.rationale: NI 81-106 sets a weekly minimum for a fund that does not use specified derivatives or sell short. A fund that uses specified derivatives or sells short must calculate NAV every business day. The monthly exception applies only to the weekly minimum.
questions.source_quote: "(a) if the investment fund does not use specified derivatives or sell securities short, once a week; (b) if the investment fund uses specified derivatives or sells securities short, once every business day." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-106-investment-fund-continuous-disclosure-nav-mer.txt NI 81-106 s.14.2(3), ~L439

questions.stem: Under the NI 81-102 risk classification method, a mutual fund's 10-year annualized standard deviation is exactly 16.0%. Which risk level applies to the fund?

options.A: Medium
options.B: Medium to high
options.C: High
options.D: Low to medium

questions.rationale: The medium band is 11 to less than 16. The medium-to-high band is 16 to less than 20. A standard deviation of exactly 16.0% is therefore in the medium-to-high band, not the medium band.
questions.source_quote: "0 to less than 6 Low 6 to less than 11 Low to medium 11 to less than 16 Medium 16 to less than 20 Medium to high 20 or greater High" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 1(1) table, ~L3655-3685

questions.stem: A new mutual fund has 3 years of returns. It is a clone fund, and its underlying fund has 12 years of history. The manager prefers to use a broad reference index for the missing years. What must the manager do?

options.A: Use the reference index, because the manager may choose any proxy.
options.B: Use only the 3 years of returns that the fund itself has earned.
options.C: Use the returns of the underlying fund for the missing 7 years.
options.D: Wait until the fund has 10 years of returns before it sets a level.

questions.rationale: A fund with less than 10 years of history fills the missing years from a proxy. A clone fund whose underlying fund has 10 years of history must use that fund's returns. A reference index applies only when no clone or matching fund exists.
questions.source_quote: "if the mutual fund is a clone fund and the underlying fund has 10 years of performance history," — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 4(1), ~L3776

questions.stem: Nadia sees a "Low" risk rating in a fund's Fund Facts. She tells her RR that the fund cannot lose money. Which reply is correct?

options.A: The rating reflects past volatility, and a low-rated fund can still lose money.
options.B: The rating guarantees that the fund will not fall in value over 10 years.
options.C: The rating measures the chance of loss, so a loss is very unlikely.
options.D: The rating is fixed at launch, so it shows the fund's future volatility.

questions.rationale: The risk level comes from the annualized standard deviation of past returns. Fund Facts must say that the rating does not show future volatility and that a low-rated fund can still lose money. The rating does not measure the chance of loss.
questions.source_quote: "It doesn’t tell you how volatile the fund will be in the future. The rating can change over time. A fund with a low risk rating can still lose money." — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part I Item 4(2)(b), ~L395

questions.stem: During the day, an ETF's market price rises well above the NAV of its holdings. Which action by authorized dealers usually moves the price back toward NAV?

options.A: They buy units on the exchange and return them to the ETF in exchange for the basket.
options.B: They ask the manager to suspend trading in the ETF until its market price falls.
options.C: They ask the manager to calculate a new NAV for the ETF at a higher value.
options.D: They deliver a basket of securities for new units and sell those units on the exchange.

questions.rationale: When the price is above NAV, authorized dealers create units with a basket and sell them, which adds supply. Buying units and redeeming them is the correct action when the price is below NAV, not above it.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.5 creation and redemption, arbitrage

questions.stem: Oskar wants to buy a thinly traded ETF. He plans to place a market order two minutes after the market opens. Which advice best protects him from paying too much?

options.A: Use a market order, because a market order always fills at the ETF's NAV.
options.B: Check the average bid-ask spread, and use a limit order or trade later in the day.
options.C: Place the order after the close, so that it fills at the next calculated NAV.
options.D: Buy a larger number of units, because a larger order narrows the spread.

questions.rationale: Prices can be more volatile near the open, and a thin market has a wide spread. A market order fills at the best price available now, not at NAV. ETF Facts suggests a limit order or a trade at another time of day.
questions.source_quote: "Consider using a limit order or placing a trade at another time" — research/sources/csa/form-41-101f4-etf-facts.txt Form 41-101F4 Part I Item 6, ~L926

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund receives unusually large redemption requests. Which cash borrowing is permitted for the fund?

options.A: A temporary loan of up to 5% of NAV to pay redemptions while it sells assets in an orderly way
options.B: A temporary loan of up to 50% of NAV from a lender that can act as a fund custodian
options.C: A permanent loan of up to 5% of NAV to buy more securities for the portfolio
options.D: A loan of up to 300% of NAV, if the fund also sells securities short

questions.rationale: A conventional mutual fund may borrow only as a temporary measure, to meet redemptions or settle trades. Its total borrowing must not exceed 5% of NAV. The 50% limit applies to alternative mutual funds and non-redeemable investment funds.
questions.source_quote: "the transaction is a temporary measure to accommodate requests for the redemption of securities of the investment fund while the investment fund effects an orderly liquidation of portfolio assets, or to permit the investment fund to settle portfolio transactions" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.6(1)(a)(i), ~L1471

questions.stem: Which feature best describes a smart-beta ETF?

options.A: It weights securities by market capitalization, like a standard broad index.
options.B: Its manager selects securities freely to beat a benchmark each year.
options.C: It follows rules that weight securities by factors such as value or low volatility.
options.D: It uses swaps to deliver twice the daily return of an index.

questions.rationale: A smart-beta index follows rules, like a passive index, but it weights securities by factors, not by market capitalization. An active manager selects securities freely. A fund that seeks a multiple of the daily return is a leveraged fund.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.6 smart beta and factor investing

questions.stem: Lena tells her dealer that her mutual fund purchase must be completed immediately. Delivery of the Fund Facts before then is not reasonably practicable. What else must the dealer do before it accepts the order?

options.A: Get her blanket written consent to later delivery of Fund Facts for all of her future purchases.
options.B: Deliver the simplified prospectus at once, because it replaces the Fund Facts for urgent orders.
options.C: Explain the Fund Facts, get her consent to later delivery for this purchase, and give a verbal summary.
options.D: Nothing more, because an urgent instruction from the client removes the Fund Facts delivery rule.

questions.rationale: The urgent-purchase exception needs more than the client's instruction. Before it accepts the order, the dealer explains Fund Facts and its delivery duty. It gets consent for that specific purchase and gives a verbal summary. A blanket consent is not valid.
questions.source_quote: "the purchaser instructs the dealer that the purchase must be completed immediately or by a specified time;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-101-mutual-fund-prospectus-disclosure.txt NI 81-101 s.3.2.02(1)(a), ~L1362

questions.stem: Thea added a large sum to a fund just before the market fell. Her annual report shows a return well below the fund's published return. Which statement best explains the gap?

options.A: Her report uses a time-weighted return, which removes the effect of her cash flows.
options.B: The fund's published return includes sales charges, but her own return excludes them.
options.C: The manager's poor decisions affected her units more than the units of other investors.
options.D: Her report uses a money-weighted return, which reflects the timing of her cash flows.

questions.rationale: A money-weighted return depends on the timing and size of deposits, so money added before a decline lowers it. The fund's published return is time-weighted, and cash flows do not affect it. Published returns also exclude sales charges.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.8 MWRR vs TWRR and exam trap

questions.stem: A rating service compares a fund with the average of its peer group. Some funds in the group closed during the period and dropped out of the data. Which problem does this cause?

options.A: Style drift, because the fund moved away from its stated investment style
options.B: Survivorship bias, because only the surviving funds remain in the average
options.C: Tracking difference, because the fund's return differed from its index return
options.D: Concentration, because the peer group now holds too few funds to compare

questions.rationale: Closed or merged funds drop out of the data, so only survivors remain, and their average looks too good. Style drift is a different problem: a fund moves away from its stated style, so its peers no longer match it.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.8 peer group, survivorship bias

questions.stem: The Larchmont Income Fund has total assets of $82,400,000 and total liabilities of $1,400,000. It has 6,000,000 units outstanding. What is its NAVPS?
questions.rationale: NAVPS = (total assets - total liabilities) / units outstanding = (82,400,000 - 1,400,000) / 6,000,000 = $13.50. The $13.73 answer ignores the liabilities, and the $13.97 answer adds them.

questions.stem: Wren invests $25,000 in a mutual fund. She pays a 4% front-end sales charge, which the dealer deducts from the amount invested. The NAVPS is $16.00. How many units does she receive?
questions.rationale: The charge is 0.04 x 25,000 = $1,000, so the net amount invested is $24,000. Units issued = 24,000 / 16.00 = 1,500. The 1,562.50 answer ignores the sales charge.

questions.stem: One year ago, a fund's NAVPS was $15.00. Today it is $15.90, after cash distributions of $0.60 per unit. What is the fund's total return per unit for the year?
questions.rationale: Total return = (ending NAVPS - beginning NAVPS + distributions) / beginning NAVPS = (15.90 - 15.00 + 0.60) / 15.00 = 10.0%. The 6.0% answer ignores the distributions, and 9.4% wrongly divides by the ending NAVPS.

questions.stem: Dmitri held 800 units of a fund one year ago at a NAVPS of $25.00. Today the NAVPS is $26.00, after cash distributions of $0.75 per unit. The fund's benchmark returned 8.5%. Which statement is correct?

options.A: His holding is worth $20,800, and the fund beat its benchmark by 1.5 percentage points.
options.B: His holding is worth $20,800, and the fund lagged its benchmark by 1.5 percentage points.
options.C: His holding is worth $21,400, and the fund lagged its benchmark by 1.5 percentage points.
options.D: His holding is worth $20,800, and the fund lagged its benchmark by 4.5 percentage points.

questions.rationale: Value = 800 x 26.00 = $20,800, because the distributions were paid in cash. Total return = (26.00 - 25.00 + 0.75) / 25.00 = 7.0%. This is 1.5 points below the 8.5% benchmark. The 4.5 answer ignores the distributions.

questions.stem: Which cost is excluded from a mutual fund's MER and shown instead in its trading expense ratio (TER)?

options.A: The trailing commission that the fund pays to the client's dealer
options.B: The management fee that the fund pays to the fund manager
options.C: Commissions that the fund pays to buy and sell its portfolio securities
options.D: The legal, audit and other operating expenses of the fund

questions.rationale: The MER covers the management fee, including any trailing commission, plus operating expenses. The fund's trading costs, such as commissions on portfolio trades, are excluded from the MER and appear in the TER.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.10 MER and TER table

questions.stem: Kofi holds a Canadian-listed ETF of U.S. dividend stocks in his TFSA. The ETF is a trust, and U.S. tax is withheld on the dividends. What is true about this withholding tax?

options.A: It is unrecoverable, because he does not report the income and so has no foreign tax credit.
options.B: It is recoverable, because the trust passes the foreign tax through to him on a T3 slip.
options.C: It is recoverable, because the tax treaty exempts all registered plans from U.S. tax.
options.D: It does not apply, because U.S. law exempts every TFSA from withholding tax on dividends.

questions.rationale: Income in a TFSA is generally tax-free, so Kofi does not report the foreign income on his return. Without reported income, he cannot claim a foreign tax credit. The T3 pass-through helps only in a non-registered account.
questions.source_quote: "any income you earn through interest, dividends or capital gains are generally tax-free" — research/sources/cra/tfsa-pages.txt CRA 'What is a TFSA', ~L167

questions.stem: Sana holds a mutual fund in a non-registered account and reinvests all distributions in new units. How are the distributions taxed?

options.A: They are tax-free, because she did not receive any cash from the fund.
options.B: They are taxable only when she redeems the new units that she received.
options.C: They reduce her ACB, so the tax is deferred until she sells her units.
options.D: They are taxable in the year she receives them, as if she had received cash.

questions.rationale: In a non-registered account, distributions are taxable whether she gets them in cash or reinvests them. The CRA considers that she received the amounts before the reinvestment. Only a return of capital reduces the ACB.
rule_refs: CRA Tax treatment of mutual funds
questions.source_quote: "Keep in mind that if you hold your fund in a non-registered account, fund distributions are included in your taxable income, whether you get them in cash or have them reinvested." — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part I Item 8, ~L695

questions.stem: Yusuf holds T-series units of a mutual fund trust in a non-registered account. Return of capital has already reduced his ACB to zero. This year he receives another $900 of return of capital. What is the tax effect?

options.A: The $900 is not taxed now, and his ACB becomes negative $900.
options.B: The $900 is taxed as interest income, and his ACB stays at zero.
options.C: The $900 is a deemed capital gain this year, and his ACB stays at zero.
options.D: The $900 is not taxed now, and he pays tax on it only at a sale.

questions.rationale: Return of capital reduces the ACB and defers tax. For mutual fund trust units, an ACB below zero gives a deemed capital gain in the year. The ACB then resets to zero, so the tax is not deferred to the sale.
rule_refs: CRA Tax treatment of mutual funds
questions.source_quote: "If the ACB of the units of the trust is reduced below zero during the tax year, the negative amount is deemed to be a capital gain in the year." — research/sources/cra/capital-gains-losses-superficial-loss-pages.txt CRA 'Tax treatment of mutual funds', ~L1696

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund holds 45% of its assets in securities listed on one foreign exchange. That exchange halts all trading for two days, and no other market trades the securities. The fund has no regulatory approval. May it suspend redemptions?

options.A: Yes, because any exchange halt lets a mutual fund suspend redemptions.
options.B: No, because the halted exchange lists less than 50% of the fund's assets.
options.C: Yes, if the fund continues to accept purchases during the suspension.
options.D: No, because a mutual fund may never suspend redemptions for any reason.

questions.rationale: Without approval, a mutual fund may suspend redemptions if trading halts on an exchange that lists more than 50% of its assets. No practical alternative market must exist. At 45%, that condition fails. A permitted suspension also bars new purchases.
questions.source_quote: "represent more than 50% by value, or underlying market exposure, of the total assets of the investment fund without allowance for liabilities and if those securities or specified derivatives are not traded on any other exchange that represents a reasonably practical alternative" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.10.6(1)(a), ~L2774

questions.stem: Ama sets up a monthly withdrawal plan from her mutual funds with her Registered Individual. Under CIRO guidance, when should a suitability determination take place?

options.A: When the plan is established, and when a triggering event occurs
options.B: Before each monthly withdrawal that the plan makes from her funds
options.C: Only at the annual account review, and not when the plan starts
options.D: At no time, because planned withdrawals are outside the suitability rule

questions.rationale: CIRO guidance says planned withdrawals need no suitability determination before each withdrawal. The Registered Individual should make one before the plan starts and when a triggering event occurs. So a review before each monthly payment is not required.
questions.source_quote: "Pre-authorized purchases or withdrawals pursuant to established plans do not require a suitability determination before each purchase or withdrawal. However, a Registered Individual should make a suitability determination before establishing a plan and when a triggering event occurs." — research/sources/ciro/gn-3400-21-004-kyc-suitability-retail-clients.txt GN-3400-21-004, ~L634

questions.stem: Ines has $8,000 to invest and can add $150 each month. She has little time or investment knowledge. Which choice is most likely suitable for her?

options.A: Three bank stocks, with a commission on each monthly purchase
options.B: A single sector fund that holds only technology stocks
options.C: An ETF bought each month, with a commission on each $150 trade
options.D: A diversified mutual fund with a pre-authorized monthly purchase plan

questions.rationale: Her small amounts cannot buy a diversified portfolio of stocks at a low cost. A diversified fund gives diversification and professional management. Small automatic purchases cost nothing extra in a mutual fund, but each ETF trade has a commission and a spread.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.12 investor decisions and RR recommendation

questions.stem: Felix has $2 million in a non-registered account, all in high-MER equity funds. He follows markets closely and wants to decide when to realize capital gains. Which recommendation best puts his interest first?

options.A: Keep the funds, because a large account gains the most from pooled management and fees.
options.B: Consider direct holdings or a managed account, and weigh the tax cost of selling the funds.
options.C: Switch to other high-MER funds that pay a higher trailing commission to the dealer.
options.D: Sell all the funds at once, because tax costs are not a factor in a recommendation.

questions.rationale: The MERs apply to his whole $2 million each year, so costs have a large impact on his returns. Direct holdings give him control of trades and of the timing of gains. The dealer must consider costs and a reasonable range of alternatives.
questions.source_quote: "the potential and actual impact of costs on the retail client’s returns, and" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3402(1)(i)(d), ~L6806

questions.stem: Which statement about a principal-protected note (PPN) that a bank issues is correct?

options.A: It pays a fixed rate of interest each year, whatever the index does.
options.B: It has no credit risk, because the issuer guarantees the principal.
options.C: Its payments link to an index, and it repays at least the amount paid for it.
options.D: It can be sold before maturity for the full amount paid, at any time.

questions.rationale: Under the Bank Act, a PPN pays amounts linked to an index or reference point and repays at least the amount paid. It may pay no interest. It still carries the issuer's credit risk, and it can be hard to sell before maturity.
questions.source_quote: "provides that the principal amount that the institution is obligated to repay at or before the note’s maturity is equal to or greater than the total paid by the person for the note." — research/sources/gov/bank-act-ppn-disclosure-extracts.txt Bank Act s.627.01 'principal-protected note', ~L41

questions.stem: Which feature defines an alternative mutual fund (a "liquid alt")?

options.A: Its objectives let it borrow, sell short or use derivatives beyond conventional fund limits.
options.B: It sells its units only to accredited investors under a prospectus exemption.
options.C: Its units trade only on an exchange, and investors have no right to redeem them.
options.D: It invests only in private companies, through a limited partnership structure.

questions.rationale: An alternative mutual fund is a public mutual fund with a prospectus. Its objectives permit commodities, crypto assets, specified derivatives, borrowing or short selling in a manner not permitted for other mutual funds. Hedge funds, not liquid alts, use prospectus exemptions.
questions.source_quote: "that has adopted fundamental investment objectives that permit it to invest in physical commodities, crypto assets or specified derivatives, to borrow cash or engage in short selling in a manner not permitted for other mutual funds under this Instrument;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.1.1 'alternative mutual fund', ~L220

questions.stem: A hedge fund charges a 20% performance fee above an 8% hurdle rate and uses a high-water mark. This year its NAVPS starts above its previous peak and rises 6%. Does the manager earn a performance fee?

options.A: Yes, because the NAVPS is above its high-water mark for the year.
options.B: Yes, on the full 6% return, because the fund had no losses this year.
options.C: No, because a performance fee applies only in the year after a loss.
options.D: No, because the return for the year is below the 8% hurdle rate.

questions.rationale: A hurdle rate is the minimum return before the manager earns any performance fee. The fund is above its high-water mark, so that test passes. But the 6% return is below the 8% hurdle, so the manager earns no performance fee.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.14 fees: management, performance, hurdle rate, high-water mark

questions.stem: Jonah had net income before taxes of $180,000 in each of the last 2 calendar years. His spouse had $140,000 in each year, and they expect similar income this year. Does Jonah meet an accredited investor income test?

options.A: No, because his own net income is below $200,000.
options.B: No, because his financial assets are not shown to exceed $1 million.
options.C: Yes, because their combined net income is more than $300,000.
options.D: Yes, because his own net income is more than $150,000.

questions.rationale: Form 45-106F9 has a combined test with a spouse. Combined net income must exceed $300,000 in each of the 2 most recent years, and be expected this year. Their total is $320,000. He fails the $200,000 individual test, but one test is enough.
questions.source_quote: "Your net income before taxes combined with your spouse’s was more than $300,000 in each of the 2 most recent calendar years" — research/sources/csa/form-45-106f9-individual-accredited-investor-risk-acknowledgement.txt Form 45-106F9 s.3, ~L55

questions.stem: In a diversified portfolio, which decision usually explains most of the variation in returns over time?

options.A: The choice of asset mix
options.B: The choice of individual securities
options.C: The timing of each trade
options.D: The commission rate on each trade

questions.rationale: The asset mix explains most of the variation in a diversified portfolio's returns, more than security selection does. So careful security selection cannot repair a mix that does not fit the client.

questions.stem: A manager uses a fixed rule. The rule raises the equity weight after markets gain and cuts it after markets fall. The manager makes no forecast. Which type of asset allocation is this?

options.A: Tactical asset allocation
options.B: Strategic asset allocation
options.C: Dynamic asset allocation
options.D: Rebalancing to fixed targets

questions.rationale: Dynamic allocation is a rule-based mix that changes automatically as market values change, such as portfolio insurance. Rebalancing does the opposite: it sells assets that rose to restore fixed targets. Tactical allocation needs a forecast.

questions.stem: A portfolio has an equity target of 60%. Its policy sets a relative band of ±5% of the target weight, not ±5 percentage points. Which equity weight is outside the band?
questions.rationale: A relative band of ±5% of a 60% target is ±3 percentage points, so the band is 57% to 63%. Only 64% is outside it. The weights 62%, 58% and 57.5% are inside the band.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.1 band illustration; 0.05 x 60 = 3 -> 57% to 63%

questions.stem: Each client below holds one type of asset for ten years. Which client is most exposed to inflation risk?

options.A: A client who holds fixed-rate GICs
options.B: A client who holds a broad equity fund
options.C: A client who holds thinly traded exempt shares
options.D: A client who holds small-cap growth stocks

questions.rationale: Fixed-rate GICs pay amounts that do not increase with prices, so inflation can reduce their real value. Thinly traded exempt shares mainly carry liquidity risk. Equities mainly carry capital risk.

questions.stem: Odalys Brennan opens an account and deposits funds. She makes no trades. Some days later, she moves all the funds to another institution. Which type of risk does this pattern show?

options.A: Liquidity risk
options.B: Issuer risk
options.C: Income risk
options.D: Financial crime risk

questions.rationale: An account used only to move funds, with no securities transactions, is an AML indicator. It shows financial crime risk, with the account as the tool. Issuer risk comes from problems at one issuer, not from how an account is used.
questions.source_quote: "Investment Dealers should be suspicious of accounts used solely as conduits to transfer funds without legitimate securities transactions." — research/sources/ciro/gn-3200-23-001-aml-compliance-guidance.txt GN-3200-23-001 s. 5.3.5, ~line 483

questions.stem: Under the PCMLTFA, when must a securities dealer report a financial transaction to FINTRAC?

options.A: When there are reasonable grounds to suspect a link to money laundering, even if the transaction is only attempted
options.B: Only when a completed transaction is above a set dollar threshold and the client is a new client
options.C: Only when the client admits that the funds come from crime and the transaction is complete
options.D: Only after CIRO reviews the transaction and tells the dealer that a report to FINTRAC is necessary

questions.rationale: PCMLTFA s. 7 requires a report of every transaction, completed or attempted, that gives reasonable grounds to suspect a listed offence. Money laundering is one such offence. The test is suspicion, not proof, an admission or CIRO approval.
questions.source_quote: "report to the Centre every financial transaction that occurs or that is attempted in the course of their activities and in respect of which there are reasonable grounds to suspect that" — research/sources/gov/pcmltfa-extracts.txt PCMLTFA s. 7, ~line 78

questions.stem: Which risk measure shows the largest fall from a previous peak to a later low that a client actually lived through?

options.A: Beta
options.B: Variance
options.C: Maximum drawdown
options.D: A multi-factor loading

questions.rationale: Maximum drawdown is the largest decline from a previous peak to a later trough in a period. Variance measures how widely returns scatter around their mean. Beta measures sensitivity to the market.

questions.stem: Two bond-heavy balanced funds have the same market beta. When interest rates rise, one fund falls much more than the other. Which measure shows this difference?

options.A: The market beta of each fund
options.B: Separate loadings on each risk factor
options.C: The ratio of each fund's beta to the market
options.D: The weighted-average beta of the two funds

questions.rationale: Multi-factor measures give a separate loading, like a beta, for each risk source, such as interest rates. Two funds with the same market beta can react very differently to rates. A single beta hides that difference.

questions.stem: Rosalind Achebe holds a Canadian equity fund. She can add one of four assets with the same expected return and standard deviation. Which correlation with her fund lowers her portfolio risk most?
questions.rationale: The lower the correlation, the larger the reduction in portfolio standard deviation. A correlation of −0.3 is the lowest of the four. A correlation near +1 gives almost no risk reduction.

questions.stem: Ewan Szabo has a large position in one stock with a large unrealized capital gain. He fears a sharp fall in the next three months. He does not want to sell this year. Which action best fits?

options.A: Sell the shares and buy a broad index fund
options.B: Buy more shares if the price falls
options.C: Buy put options on the shares he holds
options.D: Sell short shares of an unrelated company

questions.rationale: A protective put sets a minimum value for his shares and keeps his upside, less the premium. It suits a temporary concern when he has a tax reason not to sell. A sale and index purchase would diversify, but it realizes the capital gain.

questions.stem: Matthias Ferreira sells a stock short in his margin account. The price of the stock then rises a lot. What happens to the credit balance that his account must hold?

options.A: It decreases, because the short-sale proceeds grow with the price of the stock
options.B: It stays fixed, because the requirement is set on the day of the short sale
options.C: It increases, because the requirement is a percentage of the current market value
options.D: It falls to zero, because the dealer has already borrowed the shares to deliver

questions.rationale: A short position has a negative loan value equal to (100% + margin rate) times its market value. The account must hold a credit at least equal to that value (IDPC 5113). So the required credit rises with the price.
questions.source_quote: "the cash balance in the margin account must be a credit equal to or larger than the net negative loan value for the account to be in good standing" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 5113(4)(iii), ~line 14796

questions.stem: Priyanka Holloway bought 500 shares yesterday. The trade has not settled, so she has not received the shares. Today she sells them. How does UMIR treat this sale?

options.A: It is a short sale, because she has not yet received the shares
options.B: It is not a short sale, because she is deemed to own the shares
options.C: It is a short sale, unless the dealer borrows the shares first
options.D: It is not a short sale, but only if she holds a margin account

questions.rationale: Under the UMIR definition, a seller who purchased a security but has not yet received delivery is deemed to own it. So the sale is not a short sale. Borrowed shares, by contrast, do not count as owned.
questions.source_quote: "has purchased or has entered into an unconditional contract to purchase the security, but has not yet received delivery of the security" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 1.1 "short sale" (a), ~line 2467

questions.stem: Which risk applies to a client who sells a stock short but not to a client who buys the same stock?

options.A: The loss can equal the full amount invested
options.B: The client receives dividends from the issuer
options.C: The value falls if the issuer cuts its profits
options.D: The loss has no upper limit if the price rises

questions.rationale: A short seller loses as the price rises, and the price can rise without limit. A buyer can lose at most the amount invested. A short seller pays dividends on borrowed shares and does not receive them.

questions.stem: What is the starting point of the Black–Litterman model before the manager adds any views?

options.A: The market's equilibrium returns implied by market-capitalization weights
options.B: The historical average return of each asset in the portfolio
options.C: An equal weight in each asset, with no regard to correlations
options.D: A distribution of outcomes from thousands of random return paths

questions.rationale: Black–Litterman starts from market equilibrium (implied) returns from market-capitalization weights. It then blends in the manager's views, weighted by confidence. It does not start from historical averages. Random return paths describe Monte Carlo simulation.

questions.stem: Leontyne Park holds 12 stocks in equal amounts. All 12 companies are Canadian oil and gas producers. Which statement describes her portfolio?

options.A: Efficient diversification near the frontier
options.B: Naive diversification with industry concentration
options.C: Issuer concentration in one company
options.D: An allocation from the Black–Litterman model

questions.rationale: She spreads money equally across many holdings with no regard to correlations, which is naive diversification. All 12 companies react to the same news, so she has industry concentration. Issuer concentration means one oversized holding.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.6 naive diversification and concentration

questions.stem: Which asset pricing model adds a momentum factor to the three Fama–French factors of market, size and value?

options.A: The Fama–French five-factor model
options.B: The arbitrage pricing theory
options.C: The Carhart four-factor model
options.D: The capital asset pricing model

questions.rationale: The Carhart model is the three Fama–French factors plus momentum. The Fama–French five-factor model adds profitability and investment, not momentum. The CAPM uses only the market factor.

questions.stem: A small-cap value fund has a positive CAPM alpha. With a Fama–French model, its alpha is close to zero. What does this difference most likely show?

options.A: Its extra return came mostly from size and value factor exposure
options.B: Its manager has stock-selection skill that the Fama–French model hides
options.C: Its beta to the market is negative, so the CAPM understates its return
options.D: Its returns came from momentum, which the Fama–French model ignores

questions.rationale: The CAPM counts only market risk, so it labels extra return from small-cap and value stocks as alpha. The Fama–French model counts size and value as factors, and little extra return remains. So the result came from factor exposure, not skill.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.7 scenario (CAPM vs Fama-French alpha)

questions.stem: The risk-free rate is 2.5% and the expected market return is 9%. A stock has a beta of 1.4. What is its expected return under the CAPM?
questions.rationale: The market risk premium is 9% − 2.5% = 6.5%. Expected return = 2.5% + 1.4 × 6.5% = 11.6%. The 12.6% result multiplies beta by the market return, not by the premium. The 9.1% result omits the risk-free rate.

questions.stem: A portfolio holds 40% in a stock with a beta of 1.5, 35% in a stock with a beta of 0.9 and 25% in T-bills. The risk-free rate is 3% and the expected market return is 8%. What is the portfolio's CAPM expected return?
questions.rationale: Portfolio beta = 0.40(1.5) + 0.35(0.9) + 0.25(0) = 0.915. Expected return = 3% + 0.915 × 5% = 7.58%. The 7.00% result uses a simple average of the three betas. T-bills have a beta of zero but still count in the weights.

questions.stem: The risk-free rate is 4% and the expected market return is 10%. A stock has a beta of 0.8. An analyst forecasts an 8.0% return for it. Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: Required return is 8.8%; the stock plots above the SML and is undervalued
options.B: Required return is 8.8%; the stock plots below the SML and is overvalued
options.C: Required return is 8.0%; the stock plots on the SML and is fairly priced
options.D: Required return is 12.0%; the stock plots below the SML and is overvalued

questions.rationale: Required return = 4% + 0.8 × (10% − 4%) = 8.8%. The 8.0% forecast is below the required return, so the stock plots below the SML and is overvalued. The 8.0% figure multiplies beta by the market return.

questions.stem: Suppose the market is semi-strong efficient but not strong-form efficient. Which approach can still give consistent abnormal returns?

options.A: Trading on material private information
options.B: Technical analysis of past prices
options.C: Fundamental analysis of public reports
options.D: Purchases of recent top performers

questions.rationale: Semi-strong efficiency means prices reflect all public information, so technical and fundamental analysis of public data fail. Only private information can still give an edge. The strong form rules out even that.

questions.stem: Suppose the market is weak-form efficient but not semi-strong efficient. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Technical analysis of price patterns can still give abnormal returns
options.B: No approach can give abnormal returns, not even private information
